analysis.one_liner: Shields businesses and health care entities from most COVID-19 infection lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: introduced in February 2021 with no cosponsors, it sat in the House Judiciary Committee until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred almost all lawsuits against businesses, nonprofits, schools, and health care entities for damages from someone catching COVID-19 on their premises or from their services during the declared public health emergency. The shield would apply whenever the business was following federal or state reopening guidelines and CDC-style mitigation measures like mask requirements, sanitizing, social distancing, and temperature checks. The only exception was for conduct a court found to be gross negligence, and government enforcement actions were not blocked.
analysis.who_benefits: Business owners of every kind — corporations, partnerships, sole proprietors, farms, nonprofits, schools — along with health care entities treating or testing COVID patients and manufacturers or distributors of protective equipment. All would be shielded from civil suits by employees, contractors, and patrons who caught COVID-19, so long as they were operating under applicable guidelines.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Businesses and COVID-related health care entities

how_it_helps.text: The bill exempts businesses, nonprofits, educational institutions, and COVID-19 medical entities from liability for damages arising from an individual contracting COVID-19 during the public health emergency [S2][S3].

The exemption applies if the entity was operating consistent with state or federal reopening guidelines and using mitigation measures outlined by the CDC or other agencies, such as face coverings, sanitizing, social distancing, and temperature checks [S2][S3].

The shield covers employees, contractors, invitees, and any other person who visits or uses the services of a business or medical entity, and it bars compensatory, general, and punitive damages under state or federal law [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers and customers who contracted COVID-19 at a business or through a health care entity, and the families of those who died from it, would bear the cost: they would lose the ability to recover compensation through the courts unless they could prove gross negligence, a very high bar.
analysis.who_pays_short: Infected workers, patrons, and their families

drawbacks.text: The shield would leave infected employees and customers without any recovery unless a court determined the business acted with gross negligence — a standard far higher than ordinary carelessness — so even substantially careless safety practices would go uncompensated [S2][S3].

Compliance with the shield is measured against 'guidelines' rather than binding rules, which could let a business keep its immunity while following guidance that falls short of what was needed to protect people in its particular workplace [S3].
Removing the threat of lawsuits could weaken the financial incentive for businesses to invest in ventilation, paid sick leave, or other measures that reduce spread for workers and the public.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to the public is indirect at best — businesses might have reopened with more confidence fearing fewer lawsuits — while the cost is direct: people who caught a potentially fatal disease at work or in a store would have had their day in court cut off, with only a narrow gross-negligence exception. The bill shifted risk from businesses to the people least able to bear it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in February 2021 and sent to a subcommittee in April, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Budd introduced the bill on February 18, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1][S5].
On April 28, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, where it remained [S5].
No other representative cosponsored the bill during the two-year Congress [S4].
The bill never advanced beyond subcommittee referral and received no vote in either chamber before the 117th Congress ended [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers and customers kept their existing right to sue businesses and health care entities over COVID-19 infections. Businesses did not get the lawsuit shield they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers and patrons kept their right to sue

for.name: Rep. Ted Budd
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill attracted no cosponsors from either party and never reached a vote, so no party breakdown exists; it was a single Republican sponsor's measure that stalled in committee.

industries.industry: Businesses of all sizes (retail, restaurants, manufacturers, farms, nonprofits, schools)
industries.note: The bill would have given them near-complete protection from lawsuits by employees and patrons who caught COVID-19 on their premises, shifting the cost of infections onto the infected. The public's interest in holding careless employers accountable ran directly against the industry's interest here.

industries.industry: COVID-19 medical entities (providers, testers, transporters, and PPE manufacturers and distributors)
industries.note: Health care entities and equipment makers would have been shielded from suits by patients, workers, and users of their services. The gross-negligence-only exception would have left those harmed by substandard protection or care without recourse.

A broad statutory bar on COVID-19 infection claims would have sharply reduced the lawsuits insurers pay to defend and settle. Insurers did not act on the bill directly, but they are the financial intermediary for the liability the bill removed.
